questoes.pergunta: A support chatbot built on the Messages API answers its first turn correctly, but on the third turn it no longer knows which order the customer mentioned. Why must the application send the complete conversation history with each request?
opcoes: Because the model uses the earlier turns only as few-shot examples of the reply format it should follow in each new turn.
Because the API keeps no conversation state, so the model knows only what each request contains, including earlier turns.
Because the API keeps only the most recent turns server-side, so older turns must be resent to stay available to the model.
Because the API stores user turns but not tool results, so tool_result blocks must be resent on every later request.
questoes.explicacao: The Messages API is stateless: each request must carry the complete conversation history, including earlier user turns, assistant replies, and tool results, for the model to stay coherent. Sending only the latest message makes the model lose what was said before.
feedbacks: The history is not mainly a set of format examples; it is the only way the model learns what was said and done earlier in the conversation.
Correct. Without stored state, the model sees only what the request contains, so earlier turns must be resent.
The API keeps no turns at all between requests, recent or old; the full history, including the latest turns, must be in every request.
Nothing is stored server-side, neither user turns nor tool results; every earlier message must be resent, not only the tool_result blocks.

questoes.pergunta: An order lookup tool returns 45 fields per call, and the support agent uses only 5 of them. Over a long conversation with several lookups, which approach is recommended?
opcoes: Tell the agent in the system prompt to ignore the fields it does not need, so that it focuses on the five relevant fields.
Pass the full result to the agent, because the extra fields give the model more context for later turns of the conversation.
Move to a model with a larger context window, so that the accumulated lookups no longer crowd the rest of the conversation.
Trim each result to the relevant fields before it is added to the conversation, so unused fields never accumulate.
questoes.explicacao: Tool results accumulate in context and consume tokens out of proportion to their relevance. Trimming verbose tool outputs to the relevant fields before they are appended keeps the context focused; this can happen in the tool, in the loop code, or in a PostToolUse hook.
feedbacks: The ignored fields still occupy the context and still compete for attention; a prompt instruction does not remove them.
Unused fields add cost and noise on every turn and push useful facts further away; more data is not more useful context.
A larger window postpones the problem while every lookup still carries 40 irrelevant fields.
Correct. Trimming before accumulation keeps token use proportional to relevance.

questoes.pergunta: A long support conversation is progressively summarized to save space. Which information is most at risk of being lost in those summaries?
opcoes: Exact amounts, percentages, dates, and the expectations the customer stated, which tend to become vague phrases.
The overall topic of the conversation, which summaries tend to drop in favor of the most recent detailed exchange.
The system prompt instructions, which are summarized together with the history and lose their priority over time.
The tool definitions, which are removed from the request once the conversation history has been summarized once.
questoes.explicacao: Progressive summarization keeps the narrative but condenses numerical values, percentages, dates, and customer-stated expectations into vague text. Those are exactly the details that later become tool arguments or commitments to the customer.
feedbacks: Correct. Precise transactional details and stated expectations are what summaries blur.
Summaries are good at keeping the overall topic; what they lose is precision.
The system prompt is sent separately from the message history and is not part of what gets summarized.
Tool definitions are sent with each request independently of how the history is condensed.

questoes.pergunta: Where should a "case facts" block (order numbers, amounts, dates, statuses) live in a long-running support agent whose history is summarized?
opcoes: Inside the summarized history, written as a short paragraph, so that it is condensed along with the rest of the conversation.
In a separate structured log that the agent can query with a tool, so that the prompt itself stays as short as possible.
In every prompt, outside the summarized history, maintained by the application from tool results rather than by the model.
Only in the first request of the session, since the model carries the exact values forward through the later summaries.
questoes.explicacao: Transactional facts are extracted into a persistent case facts block that is included in each prompt and kept outside the summarized history. The application updates it from tool results, so exact values never pass through the summarizer.
feedbacks: Putting the facts inside the summarized text exposes them to the same condensation that blurs them.
A queryable log depends on the agent deciding to look things up; the facts need to be present in every prompt.
Correct. Included in each prompt, outside the summary, and maintained by code.
Values from the first request are exactly what later summaries condense away; the block must be repeated on every request.

questoes.pergunta: A support session involves three separate issues, each with its own order ID, amount, and status. How should these facts be kept so the agent does not mix them up?
opcoes: As one combined, structured list of all confirmed values, so the agent can scan every number of the session at once.
As one structured record per issue in a separate context layer, so each ID, amount, and status stays tied to its issue.
In the conversation summary only, so the agent sees the issues in the order the customer raised them in the session.
In three parallel sessions, one per issue, so that the agent never sees more than a single issue's values at a time.
questoes.explicacao: For multi-issue sessions, structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) is extracted and persisted in a separate context layer, one record per issue. The structure preserves which values belong together.
feedbacks: A flat list loses the association between each issue and its values, which is how amounts get applied to the wrong order.
Correct. Per-issue structured records keep IDs, amounts, and statuses together.
The summary is where precise values get blurred; it is not a safe place for transactional data.
Splitting one customer conversation into separate sessions breaks continuity and still leaves each session to manage its own facts.

questoes.pergunta: A synthesis agent receives a long aggregated input and keeps omitting findings that appear in its middle sections. Which change best mitigates this?
opcoes: Place a summary of all key findings at the beginning and organize the detailed results under explicit section headers.
Shuffle the order of the detailed results on every run, so that no single source is consistently placed in the middle.
Give the synthesis agent an explicit instruction to review its draft against the full input before replying.
Move the synthesis to a model with a larger context window, so the aggregated input fills a smaller share of it.
questoes.explicacao: Models process the beginning and end of long inputs reliably but may omit findings in the middle. Putting a key-findings summary first and structuring the details with explicit section headers mitigates this position effect.
feedbacks: Correct. Key findings up front plus explicit headers counteract lost in the middle.
Shuffling spreads the omissions across sources instead of preventing them.
A second pass over the same long input is subject to the same position effect.
The effect concerns position within the input, not the share of the window it fills.

questoes.pergunta: A downstream agent has a limited context budget and receives long, verbose reports, including reasoning chains, from several upstream agents. What should change?
opcoes: Raise the downstream agent's output token limit, so that it has more room to work through the verbose reports it receives.
Have the downstream agent write a structured summary of each upstream report first, so its later reasoning uses shorter text.
Instruct the downstream agent to skim each report and focus only on the passages that look most relevant to its own task.
Have the upstream agents return key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of verbose content and reasoning.
questoes.explicacao: When downstream agents have limited context budgets, upstream agents should return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) rather than verbose content and reasoning chains. Subagents should also include metadata such as dates, source locations, and methodological context so downstream synthesis stays accurate.
feedbacks: The output limit does not change how much input the downstream agent must hold; the reports still consume its context.
Summarizing downstream still requires reading every verbose report into the limited context first, and adds a lossy step.
Skimming instructions do not reduce the tokens that the reports occupy, and the relevant facts can still be missed.
Correct. Fixing the upstream output format keeps the downstream context for the facts that matter.

questoes.pergunta: Which observation best indicates context degradation during an extended codebase exploration session?
opcoes: The agent re-reads a file it opened an hour earlier, right after the engineer says a teammate has just pushed changes to it.
The agent's answers slow down noticeably as the session grows, although each answer still names the exact classes involved.
The agent starts describing the module in generic terms instead of naming the classes it read earlier, and contradicts itself.
The agent reports no matches for a function it described earlier, because a commit merged during the session renamed it.
questoes.explicacao: In extended sessions, degraded context shows up as inconsistent answers and references to "typical patterns" rather than the specific classes discovered earlier. Re-reading a file that just changed, slower answers that stay specific, and an empty search after a rename are expected behavior or a different issue.
feedbacks: Re-reading a file after being told it changed is correct targeted re-analysis, not forgetting.
Latency grows with context, but answers that still name the exact classes show the findings are intact; slowness alone is not the degradation symptom.
Correct. Generic descriptions in place of the classes it discovered, plus self-contradiction, are the hallmark symptoms.
This is a valid empty result caused by a real code change, not an inconsistency produced by degraded context.

questoes.pergunta: What is the main purpose of having an agent maintain a scratchpad file during a long codebase investigation?
opcoes: To persist key findings outside the conversation so the agent can reference them for later questions and after resets.
To store every tool output in full so the agent can replay the whole investigation if the session ever has to restart.
To give engineers a log to review, since the agent itself does not read files it wrote earlier in the same session.
To lower the cost of each request, since scratchpad content is automatically excluded from the context window.
questoes.explicacao: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries such as compaction, new sessions, and subagent handoffs. The agent references them for subsequent questions, which counteracts context degradation.
feedbacks: Correct. Persisted, distilled findings that the agent references are the point of the scratchpad.
Full tool outputs would make the scratchpad another verbose dump; it should hold the key findings.
The agent is meant to read the scratchpad back; that is how it counteracts degradation.
Nothing is excluded automatically; the value comes from what is written and later consulted, not from a token discount.

questoes.pergunta: A main agent coordinates a codebase investigation and needs answers to questions such as "find all test files" and "trace refund flow dependencies." How should it handle them?
opcoes: Run each search itself in the main session, so that every raw result is available when it builds the overall picture.
Delegate each question to a subagent along with the relevant prior findings, and keep only the returned summary.
Delegate each question to a subagent with only the question, since subagents inherit the main agent's findings.
Read every file in the repository first, so that later questions can be answered without any more exploration.
questoes.explicacao: Spawning subagents for specific questions isolates verbose exploration output in their own context while the main agent preserves high-level coordination. Because subagents do not inherit context, relevant findings from earlier phases are summarized and injected into their prompts.
feedbacks: Running every search in the main session floods the coordinating context with raw output.
Correct. Delegation with injected prior findings keeps the main context clean and the subagents informed.
Subagents do not inherit the main agent's context; without the prior findings they rediscover or contradict them.
Reading everything upfront wastes context; understanding should be built incrementally with targeted exploration.

questoes.pergunta: In a multi-agent workflow that may crash partway through, what does structured state persistence for crash recovery involve?
opcoes: Resuming the coordinator's conversation after a crash and asking it to recall which of the tasks it had already completed.
Restarting the whole workflow from the beginning after a crash, since no partial result from before can be trusted.
Keeping every agent inside one long session, so that the coordinator's own history holds the progress of each subagent.
Each agent exports state to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects it into prompts.
questoes.explicacao: Each agent exports its state to a known location, and on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects the relevant state into agent prompts. This turns recovery into reading structured state instead of relying on conversation memory.
feedbacks: Recalling progress from a conversation that ended mid-task is unreliable and is not structured state.
Restarting discards completed work and can overwrite results that were already correct.
Subagents run in isolated contexts, so one long session neither holds their progress reliably nor survives a crash.
Correct. Per-agent state exports plus a coordinator-loaded manifest enable recovery.

questoes.pergunta: A developer's Claude Code session is filling up with verbose Grep and file-read output during a long exploration. Which statement about /compact is correct?
opcoes: It keeps the most recent messages word for word and deletes the older ones, so that the latest tool results stay exact.
It clears the conversation entirely and starts a new empty session, keeping only the name of the previous session.
It replaces the conversation history with a summary, which reduces context usage when discovery output fills it.
It moves verbose tool outputs into a scratchpad file automatically, so that the agent can read them back later.
questoes.explicacao: /compact reduces context usage during extended exploration by replacing the conversation history with a summary, optionally focused by an instruction. Anything that must survive exactly should be kept in files such as a scratchpad, not left to the summary.
feedbacks: /compact does not preserve the recent messages verbatim; the whole conversation is replaced by a summary.
Clearing the conversation and starting empty describes /clear, not /compact.
Correct. A summary replaces the verbose history, freeing context.
/compact does not write a scratchpad; persisting findings to a file is something the agent or developer does deliberately.

questoes.pergunta: A developer wants to return to a specific investigation from two days ago in Claude Code, although several other sessions have run since then. What should she use?
opcoes: `claude --continue`, which reopens the conversation in the current directory that best matches the investigation.
`claude --resume <session-name>`, which continues that exact named conversation with its earlier context.
A fresh session with the original prompt, since sessions cannot be reopened once the terminal has been closed.
fork_session on the most recent session, which copies the earlier investigation into a new independent branch.
questoes.explicacao: Named session resumption with `--resume <session-name>` continues a specific prior conversation, which is how investigations are carried across work sessions. `--continue` only reopens the most recent session.
feedbacks: `--continue` picks the most recent session, not the one that matches a topic.
Correct. Named resumption targets the exact conversation.
Sessions are saved and can be resumed after the terminal closes.
Forking the most recent session copies that session's history, not the investigation from two days ago.

questoes.pergunta: What is fork_session designed for when managing agent sessions?
opcoes: Running the same prompt twice as independent runs and keeping whichever of the two answers turns out to be more accurate.
Moving a session to a different machine, so that another engineer can continue the work with the same history.
Creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, for example to compare two refactoring approaches.
Splitting a long session into smaller independent sessions, so that each one stays well below the context window limit.
questoes.explicacao: fork_session creates a new session that starts from a copy of an existing session's history and then diverges independently. It is used to explore divergent approaches, such as two testing or refactoring strategies, from the same analysis.
feedbacks: Forking is not a voting or best-of-two mechanism; each branch pursues a different direction.
Forking is about branching the conversation, not transferring it between machines.
Correct. Independent branches from a common baseline are the purpose of forking.
A fork starts with the full copied history, so it does not shrink the context.

questoes.pergunta: An engineer is returning to a code analysis session from last week. Which TWO practices follow the guidance on resuming versus starting fresh? Choose TWO.
opcoes: If most files are unchanged, start a fresh session with no context so the agent safely re-explores the whole codebase.
If most files are unchanged, resume the session and tell it exactly which files changed so that it re-analyzes only those.
If most analyzed files were rewritten, start a new session and inject a structured summary of the findings still valid.
In either case, fork the old session and ask the fork for a structured summary, so stale results stay in the original.
If most analyzed files were rewritten, resume anyway, since the agent re-reads every file before relying on what it knows.
questoes.explicacao: Resume when prior context is mostly valid, and inform the session about the specific file changes for targeted re-analysis. When prior tool results are stale, a new session with an injected structured summary is more reliable than resuming.
feedbacks: Discarding mostly valid context forces a full re-exploration that is unnecessary.
Correct. Mostly valid context plus a precise list of changes enables targeted re-analysis.
Correct. Stale results call for a fresh session seeded with a structured summary.
A fork copies the original history, so the stale tool results come along into the new branch.
A resumed agent trusts its earlier tool results; it does not re-read files it believes it already knows.
